questions.problem: What are the parametric equations of the hyperbola ${y}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{49}=1?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by

$$
x=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

In our case, $a=\sqrt{1}=1$ and $b=\sqrt{49}=7.$ Therefore, the parametric equations are

$$
x=7\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

questions.problem: What are the parametric equations of the hyperbola $9{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}=36?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by

$$
x=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

First, we rewrite the equation of our hyperbola in standard form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{y}^{2}-{x}^{2} & =36 \\ \frac{9{y}^{2}}{36}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{36} & =\frac{36}{36} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{36} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, in our case, $a=\sqrt{4}=2$ and $b=\sqrt{36}=6.$ Therefore, the parametric equations are

$$
x=6\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by 

$$
x=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(0,\pm a).$ From the graph, we have that $(0,1)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=1.$

Recall also that the asymptotes of the hyperbola occur at $y=\pm \frac{a}{b}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \frac{1}{2}x.
$$

Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{b} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{b} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ b & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{\sqrt{3}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{3} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{2} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{3}+1 & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Vertical Hyperbola Given Algebraically
canonical_examples.problem: What are the parametric equations of the hyperbola $\dfrac{y^2}{9} - \dfrac{x^2}{25} = 1?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{y^2}{a^2} - \frac{x^2}{b^2} = 1
$$

are given by

$$
x = b\tan{t}, \quad y = a\sec{t}.
$$

In our case, $a = \sqrt{9} = 3$ and $b = \sqrt{25} = 5.$ Therefore, the parametric equations are

$$
x = 5\tan{t}, \quad y = 3\sec{t}.
$$

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are $y=\pm 3x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\dfrac{y^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{b^2} = 1
$$

are given by 

$$
x=b\tan{t},\quad y=a\sec{t},
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(0, \pm a).$ From the graph, we have that $(0,9)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=9.$

The asymptotes of a vertical hyperbola are $y = \pm \dfrac{a}{b}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are $y = \pm 3 x,$ and so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{b} & =3 \\ \frac{9}{b} & =3 \\ b & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=3\tan{t},\quad y=9\sec{t}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations
canonical_examples.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x =2\tan{t}, \, y =3\sec{t}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the $\tan{t}$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\sec{t}$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity $\tan^2{t} + 1 = \sec^2{t}$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+1 & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
